Text: Citigroup lines up Wall Street banks for Banamex IPO Citigroup is assembling major Wall Street banks for an IPO of Mexico’s Grupo Financiero Banamex that could raise more than $3 billion, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Citigroup is expected to lead the offering, with Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase also involved. The banks are targeting January for the listing. Citigroup and Banamex are still assessing how much of Citi’s remaining stake could be sold before the IPO, with smaller stake sales possible. The plans remain under discussion and could change, while additional banks may join the syndicate. The IPO is part of CEO Jane Fraser’s broader retreat from consumer banking in international markets. Citi sold 25% of Banamex to Mexican billionaire Fernando Chico Pardo last year and another 24% to investors including General Atlantic and Blackstone, leaving it with about 51%. $C $BAC $GS $JPM

Text: Banks led by Citigroup have attracted more than $10 billion in investor orders for a leveraged-loan offering supporting Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The demand covers a $6.5 billion loan tranche, while a €1 billion tranche has drawn roughly €1.35 billion in orders, according to people familiar with the matter. Lenders are reportedly considering moving up the investor commitment deadline, currently scheduled for Wednesday, as demand exceeds the amount being offered. The loans are part of a $52 billion financing package for the transaction, the largest M&A financing package of 2026, which also includes $32 billion of investment-grade debt and the equivalent of $12.4 billion in high-yield bonds. Citigroup, Bank of America and Apollo Global Management arranged the financing earlier this year. The leveraged loans are being offered at spreads of up to 3 percentage points over benchmark rates and at 99.5 cents on the dollar. $C $BAC $APO $PSKY $WBD

Author: topstockalerts
Text: Paramount Skydance has launched its long-awaited investment-grade bond offering, the largest component of a $52 billion syndicated debt package to finance its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The company is offering senior dollar bonds across eight tranches with maturities ranging from two to 40 years, targeting about $32 billion, which would make it the fifth-largest U.S. investment-grade bond sale on record. Initial pricing discussions for the longest tranche, due in 2066, indicate a spread of roughly 3.65 percentage points over Treasurys. Apollo Global Management, Bank of America and Citigroup are leading the offering, with pricing expected Wednesday. The financing package also includes about $12.4 billion equivalent in high-yield bonds and $7.5 billion in leveraged loans, both currently being marketed. Text: Accelevation Holdings shares fell in their Nasdaq debut Wednesday after the data-center infrastructure maker and private-equity backer raised $540 million in an IPO priced below the marketed range. The stock opened at $17.55, valuing the company at about $3.9 billion. The offering included 30 million Class A shares at $18 each, with Accelevation selling 10 million and sponsor Olympus Partners 20 million. Underwriters have a 30-day option for up to 4.5 million additional shares. Accelevation will use its proceeds for debt repayment, transaction expenses and general corporate purposes, while it receives no proceeds from Olympus’ secondary sale. Customer concentration remains a risk, with two customers accounting for about 61% of direct revenue last year. Author: topstockalerts
Text: Bank of America’s Merrill Lynch unit will pay $39 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging that it paid brokerage clients near-zero interest rates instead of market rates on unused cash in retirement accounts. The preliminary settlement was filed in Manhattan federal court and requires approval from Judge Valerie Caproni. The settlement covers Merrill Edge online account holders between Dec. 15, 2016 and March 15, 2020, who allegedly received rates of 0.05%-0.14%, while some competitors paid around 2%. Merrill Lynch denied wrongdoing. In a separate case, Judge Margaret Garnett ruled that most of another class action covering retirement and non-retirement accounts can proceed. Similar lawsuits have targeted major banks and brokers over alleged cash-sweep practices that moved client funds into low-interest accounts. Merrill also agreed in January 2025 to pay $25 million to settle related SEC claims without admitting wrongdoing. $BAC
